THOUGHT: The patient is an 81-year-old male presenting with tense, non-rupturing, itchy axillary bullae, warm and inflamed surrounding skin. Key clinical clues include the location (axilla — a common site for friction and occlusion, but also relevant for certain autoimmune blistering diseases), tense bullae that do not rupture with light pressure (suggesting subepidermal blistering), and absence of systemic symptoms (e.g., fever, mucosal involvement, constitutional symptoms). The direct immunofluorescence (DIF) shows linear deposits of C3 and IgG along the basement membrane — this is the hallmark immunopathologic finding of bullous pemphigoid (BP). While linear IgG alone is highly specific for BP, the presence of both IgG and C3 further supports BP (as complement activation commonly accompanies autoantibody deposition in BP). In contrast, linear IgA disease shows IgA, and epidermolysis bullosa acquisita shows linear IgG with salt-split skin showing binding to the dermal side — neither is supported here. Pemphigus vulgaris would show intercellular (not basement membrane) IgG/C3 and flaccid (not tense) bullae that rupture easily — inconsistent with exam. Drug-induced bullous pemphigoid is well-recognized, especially in elderly patients started on new medications (e.g., dipeptidyl peptidase-4 inhibitors, penicillins, NSAIDs, PD-1 inhibitors); the timing of new medications at the assisted living facility strongly raises this possibility. His belief that poor diet caused the blisters reflects a common misconception but does not align with the objective immunopathologic and clinical findings. The normal CBC further argues against infection or hematologic malignancy as primary drivers. Age (81 years), tense bullae, pruritus, axillary (intertriginous) involvement, and DIF findings collectively make bullous pemphigoid the most likely diagnosis — likely drug-triggered given the recent medication changes.

DIAGNOSIS: Bullous pemphigoid
